levels.label: Not yet
levels.descriptor: The conclusion is stated as certain when the scenario does not support that.

levels.label: Approaching
levels.descriptor: Uncertainty is mentioned in general terms only.

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: The response says what is not known and how it limits the conclusion.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: The response says what is not known, how it limits the conclusion, and what would resolve it.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.descriptor: The criteria are not used.

levels.label: Approaching
levels.descriptor: Some criteria are used and others are dropped without saying why.

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: Every stated criterion is applied and the result of each is reported.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: Every criterion is applied and the response says which one decided the outcome.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.descriptor: The parts of the plan contradict each other or do not add up.

levels.label: Approaching
levels.descriptor: The plan adds up but one part is not connected to the rest.

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: The plan adds up and each part is consistent with the others and with the constraint.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: The plan adds up, is internally consistent, and states what would break it first.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.descriptor: A conclusion is stated with no figures behind it.

levels.label: Approaching
levels.descriptor: Figures are quoted but the step from figure to conclusion is missing.

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: The response shows which figures drive the conclusion and how.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: The response also says how large a change in a figure would flip the conclusion.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.descriptor: A choice is asserted with no cost acknowledged.

levels.label: Approaching
levels.descriptor: A choice is defended but what it gives up is not named.

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: The choice is defended and what it costs or forecloses is named specifically.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: The choice is defended, its cost is named, and the strongest case against it is answered.

judgment.prompt: Nothing in Malik’s plan goes negative, yet the purchase has a real cost beyond the money. Describe what the purchase displaces, quantify it over the life of the loan, and say what that would mean if an unexpected $900 bill arrived in month 14.
acceptableAnswerCriteria: Identifies the savings goal as what is displaced, and quantifies it as $124.00 a month or $7,440.00 over the 60 months.
Explains that a plan with $326.00 of monthly slack and no accumulated reserve has no way to absorb a $900 bill in month 14 other than borrowing or cutting a commitment.
Distinguishes a plan that balances from a plan that is resilient.
evidenceRequirements: Cites the $326.00 remaining and the $450 goal, and uses the $7,440.00 cumulative figure or an equivalent multi-month total.
lookFors: The response reasons about the reserve that was not built, not only about the monthly gap.
The month-14 case is answered with the figures rather than in general terms.
A response noting that three months of the $326.00 left over roughly equals the $900 bill is using the arithmetic well.
judgment.commonMisconception: Treating "the numbers balance" as the same thing as "this is affordable".

judgment.prompt: The payment alone reads as 13.7% of take-home pay and the full cost reads as 22.5%. Explain which of the two a lender is more likely to use and why, and say what that means for a buyer reading a lender’s approval as advice.
acceptableAnswerCriteria: Explains that a lender is assessing whether its own payment will be made, so the $389 figure is the one relevant to its decision.
Concludes that an approval answers a narrower question than "can I afford this", so a buyer should not read it as a judgement about the whole $639.00 commitment.
evidenceRequirements: Uses both percentage figures, 13.7% and 22.5%, when explaining the difference in what each measures.
lookFors: The response treats the lender as answering a legitimate but different question rather than as acting in bad faith.
The response says what the buyer should do with the approval, not just that it is incomplete.
judgment.commonMisconception: Reading a lending decision as a verdict on whether a purchase is affordable.

oracle.method: every fixed answer above was recomputed from the item's own stated scenario parameters, not transcribed
oracle.arithmetic: exact rational arithmetic over BigInt; no binary floating point
oracle.limits: Recomputation establishes that the key follows from the stated figures. It does not by itself establish that the model chosen is the right model for the scenario; that is carried by the per-item reasoning, the parameter-visibility check, and human review.
